title: Transformer Lead Times Top 160 Weeks for US AI Data Centers
summary:
A shortage of utility-ready buildings and electrical equipment is leaving billions of dollars in GPU hardware unused as the U.S. artificial intelligence buildout hits a power wall. The lead time for generator step-up transformers exceeded 160 weeks in the first quarter of 2026, while high-voltage circuit breaker lead times rose to 125 weeks from 77 weeks in 2023. This gap between rapid chip delivery and multi-year electrical construction has left neocloud provider Nscale with only 25,000 operational GPUs as of Aug. 31, despite having 461,000 contracted.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that a lack of "warm shells"—empty buildings near large power feeds—could result in piles of chips sitting idle without power. To counter the deficit, OpenAI is lobbying the U.S. government for 100 GW of additional power generation annually. Meanwhile, GE Vernova reported its gas equipment backlog grew to 116 GW in one quarter, with some turbines not expected to arrive until 2031. SoftBank-controlled SB Energy, which is developing an Ohio site for OpenAI, has shifted its IPO timeline to December or possibly 2027.

selectedTweets.text:
Satya Nadella already said last year that the company doesn’t have enough electricity to power all its AI GPUs. 
He said they might end up with a pile of chips just sitting around because there’s not enough power to plug them in.

The issue is not supply of chips but missing “warm shells” (empty but utility-ready building ), meaning finished data center buildings near large power feeds.

OpenAI is pushing the U.S. government to add 100 gigawatts per year of generation as a strategic asset for AI.

This power gap creates stranded capital since GPUs depreciate while waiting for buildings, substations, and transmission to be ready.

Even if training stays centralized, inference demand is the big driver for electricity, so any shift of queries to efficient edge devices would change grid and data center sizing assumptions.

The main problem is, power delivery and construction schedules run on multi-year permitting and build cycles, while GPU supply ramps in quarters.

selectedTweets.bestBit: Bernstein estimates just 35% of the planned US pipeline is actually credible
selectedTweets.text:
Holy, The FT’s deep dive into America’s AI infrastructure boom is brutal: at least 47 major US data center projects have already been delayed, withdrawn or blocked in 2026, while more than 1,000 communities have tried to restrict new projects.

Bernstein estimates just 35% of the planned US pipeline is actually credible.

And the amount of capital required is staggering. Columbia economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the AI buildout will require $10.3 TRILLION through 2032, averaging 3.63% of US GDP every year, larger relative to GDP than the railroad, highway or telecom booms.

One of the biggest bets already has an escape hatch: Anthropic can terminate affected orders in its up-to-$44.6B deal with Nvidia-backed Nscale if financing or delivery deadlines are missed. Nscale had just 25,000 GPUs operational in August versus 461,000 active and contracted, while targeting a ~$35B IPO.

Then there’s SoftBank-backed SB Energy.

It has completed ZERO data centers, but needs about $174B to fulfill roughly $430B in contracted future revenue, much of it tied to OpenAI. Its planned ~$50B IPO has already been delayed.

The scramble for compute is already lowering the bar: OpenAI and Anthropic have increasingly accepted higher costs and less-experienced developers simply to secure compute fast enough.

The AI buildout being discussed is measured in trillions. The question is increasingly whether the companies promising all that capacity can actually finance and deliver it.
